step1.title: Build the list
step1.body: Names and emails. We flag duplicates and addresses that look mistyped.

step2.title: Add the details
step2.body: A prize, or a suggested budget, date and place for the exchange. You can leave a note for the group.

step3.title: Spin and send
step3.body: The wheel runs the ceremony and the emails go out on their own. If one bounces, retry just that one.

fairness.title: The animation decides nothing
fairness.lede: It is the classic trick with wheels on the web: the spin looks lovely but the result was written in advance, or worse, the browser's physics picked it.

point1.title: The server decides
point1.body: The winner comes from a cryptographic generator on the server. The animation is calculated afterwards to land exactly on that segment.

point2.title: No modulo bias
point2.body: Numbers that would fall outside the range are thrown away and drawn again, so no participant ends up with better odds than another.

point3.title: Verifiable ID
point3.body: Every draw stores a hash of its seed and timestamp. We hand you that identifier so you can show the draw was not re-run until the right name came up.

privacy.title: Only what the draw needs
privacy.point1: We only ask for a name and an email. No accounts, no passwords.
privacy.point2: Secret Santa assignments are stored encrypted and deleted once the emails are out.
privacy.point3: Participant emails are deleted after 3 days; 10 at most.

finalCta.title: Fate has spoken
finalCta.body: Well, almost: you still have to build the list.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.intro: This isn't a contract full of small print. It's what we do with your data, said plainly.

s1.title: What we keep
s1.body: Only what the draw needs: each person's name and, when emails are going out, their address. Whoever organises can add their own address to get the summary. No account, no password, no date of birth, nothing that doesn't go on the wheel.

s2.title: What we use it for
s2.body: Running the draw and sending the result. That's it. We don't sell data, build profiles or send marketing. If you choose not to email anyone in raffle mode, we don't even ask for addresses.

s3.title: How long
s3.body: Email addresses are deleted on their own, and soon. If the draw went out with no failures, after 72 hours: the assignments already travelled by email and there is nothing left to do with those addresses. If a delivery failed, they are kept 10 days at most, which is what keeps the retry possible. A scheduled job does it every day; it doesn't depend on anyone remembering.

s4.title: Secret Santa
s4.body: Who gives to whom is stored encrypted with AES-GCM and the key lives only on our server. Neither the organiser nor we can read it from the database. Once every email has gone out, those rows are deleted: the assignment exists only in each person's inbox.

s5.title: Who we share it with
s5.body:
Four services, and only what they need:

• Resend, to send the emails. It gets the recipient's name and address.
• Neon, the Postgres where draws live.
• Cloudflare Turnstile, the captcha that stops people using this to send spam. It doesn't use tracking cookies.
• Adsterra, the network that serves the ads. It is what pays for the hosting and the emails.

Every ad loads inside an isolated frame that cannot read anything on this page: not your list, not the addresses you typed, not your form draft. What the network does see is what any ad network sees: your browser, roughly which country you are in, and which page you were on.

There's no analytics of our own, no pixels of ours, no social widgets. The privacy and terms pages carry no ads.

s6.title: Cookies
s6.body:
We set none ourselves. We keep three things in your browser's local storage, which never leave your device: whether you prefer day or night mode, whether you want sound, and your form draft so you don't lose it on reload.

The ad network does set its own, which is how advertising on the internet works. We have no access to them and use them for nothing. You can clear them, and block them, from your browser settings; the draw works exactly the same with an ad blocker on.

s7.title: Your rights
s7.body: You can ask us to delete your address before the window is up, or to tell you what we hold. Write to {email} with the draw ID at hand, which is what lets us find it.

terms.title: Terms
terms.intro: Short rules for a short tool.

s1.title: What this is
s1.body: A free tool for raffles and Secret Santa. No accounts, no payments, no guaranteed support.

s2.title: Acceptable use
s2.body: You may only add email addresses of people who know they're taking part. Using this to email people who aren't expecting it is spam, and we cut access without notice. That's exactly why there's a limit on draws per hour.

s3.title: The emails
s3.body: We send one email per person, from a verified sender, with a footer to report it. If someone marks your email as spam it can affect delivery of later ones, so tell your group before you run the draw.

s4.title: No warranties
s4.body: The service is offered as is. We do our best to keep the draw fair and the emails delivered, but we can't guarantee every mail provider will accept them, or that the service is always up.

s5.title: Liability
s5.body: We're not responsible for gifts that never arrived, prizes that weren't handed over or exchanges that went sideways. The wheel decides; the rest is between you and your group.

s6.title: Changes
s6.body: If these terms change, the date above changes. Carrying on using the site after a change means accepting it.

faq.title: What people usually ask
faq.lede: Straight answers. If one is missing, write to us.

q1.q: How do you run a Secret Santa online?
q1.a:
You type the names and emails of everyone taking part, set the suggested budget, the date and the place of the exchange, and spin. Each person gets an email telling them who they're buying for.

Nothing to install, no account. The minimum group is three people and the maximum is fifty.

q2.q: Can the organiser see who got whom?
q2.a:
No. That's the main difference from doing it with slips of paper: whoever hands them out always ends up seeing something.

The assignment is computed on the server and stored encrypted with AES-GCM. The key never leaves the server, so not even database access reveals it. Once every email has gone out, those rows are deleted: from then on the assignment exists only in each person's inbox. The organiser's screen only says whose turn it is, never who they're buying for.

q3.q: Is the wheel draw actually random?
q3.a:
Yes, and the animation has nothing to do with it. That's the usual trick with wheels on the web: the spin looks lovely but the result was written in advance, or the browser's physics picked it.

Here the winner comes from a cryptographic generator (crypto.getRandomValues) and the animation is calculated afterwards to land exactly on that segment. Numbers that would fall outside the range are thrown away and drawn again, so no participant ends up with better odds because of a division remainder.

q4.q: How many people can take part?
q4.a:
Between 3 and 50 for Secret Santa, and between 2 and 50 for a simple raffle.

The minimum of three for Secret Santa isn't arbitrary: with two people the exchange is obvious and there's no secret left to keep.

q5.q: Can you stop a couple from getting each other?
q5.a:
Yes. In the details step you can add exclusions: pairs of people who shouldn't be matched. It works both ways, so excluding Ana from Kenji also excludes Kenji from Ana.

If the exclusions leave no possible draw, you're told before you spin, not after.

q6.q: Why does one exclusion break a three-person draw?
q6.a:
Because with three people there are only two valid arrangements, and each one uses one of the two directions of every pair.

With A, B and C the only possibilities are A→B→C→A and A→C→B→A. Exclude A from C and the first falls because it contains C→A, the second because it contains A→C. Nothing is left. From four people up there's room; with three, none.

q7.a: No. No sign-up, no password, no email verification to use it. You type the list and spin.

q8.q: What happens to the participants' emails?
q8.a:
They're deleted automatically 30 days after the draw. A scheduled job does it every day; it doesn't depend on anyone remembering.

They're not sold, not used for advertising, and not shared with anyone except the service that sends the emails.

q9.a:
For a simple raffle, yes: you can choose to email nobody and read the result on screen, which is the practical option when everyone is in the room.

For Secret Santa email is required, because it's the only place the result can appear without the rest of the group seeing it.

q10.q: What is a derangement and why does it matter here?
q10.a:
A derangement is a permutation where no element stays in its original position. Applied to Secret Santa: an arrangement where nobody draws their own name.

It's the property any properly built Secret Santa has to satisfy, and the reason shuffling the list and pairing by position isn't enough: that way someone draws themselves once in every e times, which is nearly 37% of the time.
